title: Transoral Submandibular / Parotid Duct Stone Removal (Sialodochotomy)
source_label: Atlas of Head and Neck Surgery (Simo, Pracy, Fernandes 2024) and Pasha 6e
indications: Gland-preserving open removal of salivary stones that are palpable or too large for endoscopic basket retrieval. Typical indications are submandibular stones in the distal, middle or hilar duct (often larger than about 6 mm, palpable, impacted), and anterior-third Stensen duct stones. Performed after acute infection has settled, when conservative care (hydration, massage, warm compresses, sialogogues) fails. Small mobile stones (up to about 4 mm submandibular, 3 mm parotid) suit sialendoscopy; intraparenchymal stones may need fragmentation, a combined approach or gland excision.
setup: High-resolution ultrasound to size and localize the stone; CT or cone-beam CT if ultrasound is unclear
Local anesthesia for distal palpable stones; general anesthesia with nasotracheal intubation for hilar or posterior stones
Ferguson-type mouth prop on the contralateral side to allow tongue retraction (not a bite block that fixes the tongue)
Lacrimal probes and dilators, sialendoscope if available, dental excavator, 20 mL saline syringe with soft tip
Fine sutures (6-0 and 4-0 absorbable), stents for Stensen duct (fine silicone tube or cannula)
Consent for lingual nerve injury, bleeding, duct stenosis, ranula, and residual stones
landmarks: Sublingual gland as a yellowish ridge lateral to the planned incision
Wharton duct on the medial undersurface of the sublingual gland
Lingual nerve crossing beneath the duct from lateral to medial near the second molar
Ranine veins and lingual artery medially
Stensen papilla opposite the upper second molar; buccal branch of facial nerve along the duct
danger: Lingual nerve in the posterior floor of mouth (hilar danger zone)
Pushing the stone backward into the gland during manipulation
Ranine and lingual vessel bleeding; avoid monopolar near the nerve
Incising into the sublingual gland (postoperative ranula)
Stensen duct stenosis after opening it without stenting
Leaving fragments in the floor of mouth
steps: Position and expose

Place the mouth prop on the opposite side and retract the tongue away with the nondominant index finger over gauze, which straightens the duct and lifts the floor of mouth. Palpate bimanually to locate the stone and confirm it matches the imaging. Loupes help.
Infiltrate

Inject local anesthetic with adrenaline superficially along the planned incision. This reduces bleeding and hydrodissects the submucosal plane above the duct, sublingual gland and nerve. Keep the volume small so the stone remains palpable and the anatomy is not distorted.
Secure a distal stone

For a palpable stone in the anterior or middle duct, pass a stay suture around the duct just behind the stone to stop it migrating back toward the gland. Cannulating the papilla with a probe helps define the duct course.
Incise directly over a distal stone

Incise the mucosa and duct longitudinally directly over the stone with a blade, staying parallel to the duct. Deliver the stone with a fine elevator or excavator under direct vision and irrigate the duct to flush retained saliva or debris.
Marsupialize or leave open

Suture the cut duct edges to the oral mucosa with fine interrupted absorbable sutures to create a new wide opening, which reduces stricture. Releasing the stay suture and massaging the gland confirms free salivary flow.
Retropapillary incision for hilar stones

For a proximal or hilar stone, start an incision about 5 mm behind the papilla, medial to the sublingual gland, and carry it back to the first or second molar. Cut mucosa only; a deeper first cut risks the duct, nerve, vessels and tongue muscle.
Follow the duct posteriorly

Develop the loose areolar plane and identify the duct on the undersurface of the sublingual gland. A retraction suture in the sublingual gland pulled anterolaterally lifts the duct. Follow the duct back with blunt dissection and bipolar hemostasis.
Free the lingual nerve

Behind the first molar, find the lingual nerve where it crosses under the duct from lateral to medial; this is usually where hilar stones sit. Separate nerve from duct carefully, as prior inflammation causes adhesions. Keep the nerve in view during the ductal incision.
Bring the hilum forward

Have the assistant press the submandibular gland upward and forward from the neck, delivering the hilum and stone toward the mouth. Brief the assistant to hold steady, because losing this pressure loses the stone and the plane.
Open the duct and extract

Incise the duct directly over the stone, extending past its anterior edge, on the side of the nerve that keeps it safe. Lift the stone out with an excavator, then irrigate through the duct; this often brings smaller stones forward. Collect every fragment.
Close

Approximate the duct edges with 6-0 absorbable suture where feasible; leaving a proximal ductotomy open rarely causes problems. Close the floor-of-mouth mucosa loosely with 4-0 absorbable sutures. Rinsing the bed with tranexamic acid and a single steroid dose can limit swelling.
Anterior Stensen duct stone

Cannulate the parotid papilla with a probe until it meets the stone, make an elliptical incision around the papilla, and dissect along the duct to the stone. Open the duct over the stone, deliver it, massage the gland, and stent the duct with sutures to the buccal mucosa, or marsupialize the opening.
exit_check: All stones and fragments retrieved; clear saliva flows on gland massage
Lingual nerve seen intact; floor-of-mouth hemostasis secure
Stensen duct stented or marsupialized if opened
postop: Often day case; admit overnight if floor-of-mouth or neck swelling is significant, watching the airway
Analgesia with NSAIDs; cold soft diet and at least 2 L of fluid daily
Avoid sialogogues for the first few days, then use them with massage to flush the gland
Review at 10 to 14 days (sutures, stent removed at about 2 weeks) and at 2 to 3 months for stenosis and recurrence

late: Duct stricture, especially of Stensen duct

attending_followup: Why is the submandibular gland the most common site of stones?

Its duct is long and runs uphill against gravity, its saliva is more alkaline and mucinous with higher calcium content, and its papilla is narrow. About 80 to 90 percent of stones occur there, and most submandibular stones are radiopaque, whereas most parotid stones are radiolucent.
Where does the lingual nerve relate to Wharton duct?

It starts lateral to the duct near the third molar, crosses beneath it from lateral to medial at about the second molar, and then runs medially into the tongue. This crossing zone is where hilar stones are typically removed and where nerve injury is most likely.
Which stones suit sialendoscopy versus open removal?

Small mobile stones (up to about 4 mm submandibular, 3 mm parotid) suit basket retrieval. Intermediate stones may need laser or mechanical fragmentation. Large, impacted or palpable hilar submandibular stones are well suited to transoral release; inaccessible intraparenchymal stones may need a combined approach or gland excision.
Why stent the parotid duct after opening it?
Stensen duct is narrow and prone to stenosis when the papilla or duct is incised. A temporary stent for about two weeks, or marsupialization, keeps the lumen open while it heals.
What is the key maneuver for hilar stone release?

Bimanual pressure: an assistant pushes the submandibular gland up from the neck, bringing the hilum and stone forward into the floor of mouth, so the stone can be removed under direct vision with the lingual nerve protected.
